title: A warmer lagoon
blurb: How much warmer is the air over the Venice Lagoon than in 1981?
narrative: Open the case: air temperature over the Venice Lagoon, Italy, since 1981.
Check the evidence: when did the warming become impossible to dismiss?
Call the line-up: what else changed in the same air?
Look at the map: is the Adriatic coast alone, or the whole region?

variable.name: Air temperature
variable.definition: How warm the air is about 2 metres above the ground, averaged over day and night.

emergence.explanation: The trend first became statistically clear in 2000, when the record was 20 years long, and it has stayed clear ever since.

verdict.headline: Case closed: air temperature is rising.
verdict.how_much: +0.413 °C per decade (Sen's slope); the fitted line changes by +1.78 °C over the whole period (+12%).
verdict.how_sure: Both tests agree this is very unlikely to be chance (t-test p < 0.001, Mann-Kendall p < 0.001).

limitations: Values come from MERRA-2, a global reanalysis (a weather model corrected with observations), on a grid of roughly 50 km: they describe the area around the point, not the exact spot.
Only straight-line trends are tested. A change that speeds up, slows down or reverses is not captured.

Years that resemble the one before them make the tests over-confident. When the lag-1 autocorrelation is above 0.3 in absolute value, the verdict uses the Mann-Kendall p-value corrected for it (Hamed and Rao, 1998); the t-test p-value is never corrected.
The line-up, the trend map and the emergence year use the Mann-Kendall p-value without the autocorrelation correction.
A trend shows that a value changed, not why it changed.

variable.name: Evaporation from land

variable.name: Topsoil wetness
variable.definition: How wet the top 5 cm of soil is, from 0 (completely dry) to 1 (soaked).

variable.name: Precipitation
variable.definition: How much water falls from the sky as rain or snow, on an average day.

variable.name: Root-zone soil wetness

variable.name: Air pressure
variable.definition: The weight of the air pressing down on the ground.

variable.name: Wind speed
variable.definition: How fast the air moves 10 metres above the ground.

variable.name: Temperature swing
variable.definition: The gap between the hottest and the coldest hour of the day, on average.

variable.name: Wind speed higher up
variable.definition: How fast the air moves 50 metres above the ground, the height of a wind turbine.

variable.name: Cloud cover
variable.definition: The share of the sky covered by clouds.

variable.name: Snow depth
variable.definition: How deep the snow lying on the ground is.

variable.name: Snow cover
variable.definition: The share of the land covered by snow, from 0 (none) to 1 (all).

variable.name: Snowfall
variable.definition: How much water falls as snow over land, on an average day.

variable.name: Air temperature anomaly (GISTEMP)
variable.definition: How much warmer or colder than the 1951–1980 average the air near the ground was, from land weather stations and ocean ships and buoys, spread over a 2° grid.

agreement.text: All witnesses point the same way (up) and every trend is significant.

limitations: The witnesses are built differently (a reanalysis, a gridded record of stations and ships, single stations), but they may rely on some of the same observations. How independent they are has not been fully established, so agreement between them is not proof.
The witnesses are compared over their common period only (1981–2025), so these trends can differ from the ones over each record's full length.
The correlation includes any trend the series share, so it can be high even when their year-to-year ups and downs do not match.
Only straight-line trends are tested. A change that speeds up, slows down or reverses is not captured.

Years that resemble the one before them make the tests over-confident. When the lag-1 autocorrelation is above 0.3 in absolute value, the verdict uses the Mann-Kendall p-value corrected for it (Hamed and Rao, 1998); the t-test p-value is never corrected.

GISTEMP is an anomaly from the 1951–1980 average, while MERRA-2 is an absolute temperature: their levels differ, so only trends and year-to-year changes are compared (slopes are in the same unit, °C per decade).
A GISTEMP cell is 2° wide (about 200 km) and spreads station and ship data up to 1,200 km, while a MERRA-2 cell is 0.5° (about 50 km): the two describe areas of different sizes.
